2	
3	import (
4		"context"
5		"fmt"
6		"log/slog"

9		"strings"

12		"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/settings"
13	)
14	
15	// CheckpointSyncRemoteSource identifies which precedence rule elected the
16	// checkpoint sync remote.
17	type CheckpointSyncRemoteSource string
18	
19	const (
20		// SyncRemoteSourceConfig: strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote.
21		SyncRemoteSourceConfig CheckpointSyncRemoteSource = "config"
22		// SyncRemoteSourceDefault: "origin" exists.
23		SyncRemoteSourceDefault CheckpointSyncRemoteSource = "default"
24		// SyncRemoteSourceSole: exactly one remote configured.
25		SyncRemoteSourceSole CheckpointSyncRemoteSource = "sole"
26		// SyncRemoteSourceFirst: first remote in .git/config order.
27		SyncRemoteSourceFirst CheckpointSyncRemoteSource = "first"
28	)
29	
30	// CheckpointSyncRemote is the single git remote elected to carry checkpoint
31	// data. Name is empty when no remotes are configured.
32	type CheckpointSyncRemote struct {
33		Name   string
34		Source CheckpointSyncRemoteSource
35	}
36	
37	// ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote elects the one configured git remote that
38	// checkpoint data syncs to. Pure local lookup — no network. Precedence:
39	// checkpoint_push_remote setting (fail-closed if the named remote does not
40	// exist), then "origin", then the sole remote, then the first remote in
41	// .git/config order. It knows nothing about the checkpoint_remote URL
42	// feature; callers exempt that case themselves.
43	//
44	// Deliberately NOT keyed on the branch's tracking config
45	// (branch.<name>.pushRemote / remote.pushDefault / branch.<name>.remote).
46	// Election is compared against the remote of the push actually being made, so
47	// electing the tracking remote silently drops checkpoint sync on every push to
48	// any OTHER remote — `git push <other> HEAD`, a `git clone -o base` whose
49	// checkpoints go to a separately added origin, any repo with remote.pushDefault
50	// set. TestAlternates_RelativeObjectAlternate_CheckpointSync is the regression:
51	// it clones with `-o base` and pushes checkpoints to `origin`, and a tracking
52	// tier makes the pre-push hook a silent no-op.
53	//
54	// The fork setup that motivated the tracking tier — clone the base repo, add
55	// your fork, push there, with origin unpushable — is served by setting
56	// checkpoint_push_remote explicitly. That is also the only form of it that
57	// works end to end: read paths (resume, explain) resolve checkpoints through
58	// origin's remote-tracking refs, so a silently elected non-origin remote
59	// produces checkpoints that cannot be read back from the same clone.
60	func ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote(ctx context.Context) (CheckpointSyncRemote, error) {
61		// Fail closed on an unreadable settings file: election must never
62		// override a checkpoint_push_remote the file may contain but we could
63		// not read, or checkpoints would silently re-route away from the remote
64		// the user configured for isolation.
65		s, err := settings.Load(ctx)
66		if err != nil {
67			return CheckpointSyncRemote{}, fmt.Errorf("cannot read settings to resolve the checkpoint sync remote: %w", err)
68		}
69		if name := s.GetCheckpointPushRemote(); name != "" {
70			if !isConfiguredRemote(ctx, name) {
71				return CheckpointSyncRemote{}, fmt.Errorf(
72					"checkpoint_push_remote %q is not a configured git remote; checkpoint sync disabled until fixed", name)
73			}
74			return CheckpointSyncRemote{Name: name, Source: SyncRemoteSourceConfig}, nil
75		}
76	
77		remotes := configuredRemotesInConfigOrder(ctx)
78		switch {
79		case len(remotes) == 0:
80			return CheckpointSyncRemote{}, nil
81		case slices.Contains(remotes, "origin"):
82			return CheckpointSyncRemote{Name: "origin", Source: SyncRemoteSourceDefault}, nil
83		case len(remotes) == 1:
84			return CheckpointSyncRemote{Name: remotes[0], Source: SyncRemoteSourceSole}, nil
85		default:
86			return CheckpointSyncRemote{Name: remotes[0], Source: SyncRemoteSourceFirst}, nil
87		}
88	}
89	
90	// checkpointSyncAllowedForRemote reports whether a push to pushRemote may
91	// carry checkpoint data. False for every remote except the elected
92	// checkpoint sync remote — including raw-URL pushes (git passes the URL as
93	// the hook arg) and the fail-closed misconfigured case. Callers exempt the
94	// dedicated checkpoint_remote URL mode before calling.
95	func checkpointSyncAllowedForRemote(ctx context.Context, pushRemote string) bool {
96		syncRemote, err := ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote(ctx)
97		if err != nil {
98			// Neutral wording: err covers both a misconfigured checkpoint_push_remote
99			// and an unreadable settings file, and the wrapped error already carries
100			// the specifics.
101			logging.Warn(ctx, "checkpoint sync skipped: cannot resolve checkpoint sync remote",
102				slog.String("error", err.Error()))
103			return false
104		}
105		if syncRemote.Name == "" || syncRemote.Name != pushRemote {
106			logging.Debug(ctx, "checkpoint sync skipped: push remote is not the checkpoint sync remote",
107				slog.String("push_remote", pushRemote),
108				slog.String("checkpoint_sync_remote", syncRemote.Name))
109			return false
110		}
111		return true
112	}
113	
114	// configuredRemotesInConfigOrder lists remote names in .git/config section
115	// order (approximates "first remote added"; `git remote` output is
116	// alphabetical and unsuitable). Remotes configured with only pushurl are
117	// deliberately invisible (spec Unit 1). Errors yield an empty list.
118	func configuredRemotesInConfigOrder(ctx context.Context) []string {
119		out, err := exec.CommandContext(ctx, "git", "config", "--local", "--get-regexp", `^remote\..*\.url$`).Output()
120		if err != nil {
121			return nil
122		}
123		var names []string
124		seen := map[string]bool{}
125		for _, line := range strings.Split(strings.TrimSpace(string(out)), "\n") {
126			// line: "remote.<name>.url <url>"; <name> may contain dots, so trim
127			// the fixed prefix and the ".url <value>" suffix instead of splitting.
128			key, _, ok := strings.Cut(line, " ")
129			if !ok {
130				continue
131			}
132			name := strings.TrimSuffix(strings.TrimPrefix(key, "remote."), ".url")
133			if name == "" || name == key || seen[name] {
134				continue
135			}
136			seen[name] = true
137			names = append(names, name)
138		}
139		return names
140	}

content.text:
Yes — intentional, but only in one of the shapes, and the diagnostics for it are thin.

## What changed

`entire` now elects **one** remote to carry checkpoint data and skips checkpoint sync on a push to anything else (`cmd/entire/cli/strategy/checkpoint_sync_remote.go:60`, gate at `manual_commit_push.go:84`). Landed in v0.10.0 (commit `3ef4422c5`, ENT-1451). Election order:

1. `strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote` (fail-closed if the named remote doesn't exist)
2. `origin`, if it exists
3. the sole remote
4. first remote in `.git/config` order

Notably, the branch's tracking config is deliberately *not* a tier — `101b32853` added it, `74e239a9d` took it back out.

## So whether you lost sync depends on shape

| Your setup | Checkpoints sync? |
|---|---|
| One remote, named `upstream` (no `origin`) | **Yes** — tier 3 elects it |
| `origin` exists, you push to `fork` / have `remote.pushDefault=fork` / `branch.X.pushRemote=fork` | **No** — elects `origin`, your push goes elsewhere |
| Several remotes, none called `origin`, you push to the one that isn't first in `.git/config` | **No** |
| `git push https://…` (raw URL) | **No**, by design |

Just "the remote isn't called origin" is fine. What breaks it is `origin` existing (or being config-order-first) while you push somewhere else. I confirmed both halves against the integration suite — `TestCheckpointSyncRemote_DefaultElection_OnlyOriginReceivesCheckpoints` and `TestCheckpointSyncRemote_BranchTrackingDoesNotReroute` pass, i.e. the non-elected remote receives nothing.

## Fix for the affected repos

```json
{ "strategy_options": { "checkpoint_push_remote": "fork" } }
```

in `.entire/settings.json` (or `settings.local.json`). `entire status` then prints `Checkpoints sync to: fork (set by checkpoint_push_remote)`.

## Two things worth calling out as real gaps

**Discoverability.** In the broken shape nothing warns. The pre-push hook returns `nil` after a `logging.Debug` line; `entire status` cheerfully says `Checkpoints sync to: origin` and lets the unpushed counter climb, and `entire doctor` doesn't check this at all (only `doctor migrate` consults the resolver). The user-visible signal for "your pushes are silently carrying no checkpoints" is a number that grows. A doctor check comparing the elected remote against the push destination git would actually use — including `remote.pushDefault` and `branch.<name>.pushRemote` — would turn this from "user files a report" into "doctor tells you and offers the setting."

**The workaround isn't fully wired.** Setting `checkpoint_push_remote=fork` fixes the push, but reads bootstrap only from `origin`'s remote-tracking ref (`checkpoint/persistent.go:2233`, `resume.go:873`), and repo identity for the API keys on `origin` too (`entireapi_client.go:78`). So checkpoints land in the fork while a fresh clone's read path looks for them under `origin/…`. That's also why the sole-remote case works for pushing but would not read back from a `git clone -o upstream`. The election comment in the source acknowledges this as the reason for excluding the tracking tier — it's an honest constraint, not an oversight, but it means non-`origin` setups are only half-supported.

Want me to file these two, or write the doctor check?
would you see this in entire doctor?
Let me verify rather than restate — I'll check what doctor actually inspects.

23	// at `entire enable` and on demand from `entire doctor` rather than letting
24	// someone discover it when a resume comes up empty.
25	
26	// remoteDestination is one remote and what checkpoints pushed to it would do.
27	type remoteDestination struct {
28		name string
29		// pushURLs are the URLs a push to this remote delivers to, in git's order.
30		pushURLs []string
31		// pinned reports that remote.PushURL resolves this remote to a configured
32		// checkpoint_remote, so its own push URLs are irrelevant to checkpoints.
33		//
34		// Asked of the resolver rather than derived from settings on purpose: a
35		// checkpoint_remote that is *present* is not necessarily *in effect* —
36		// PushURL falls back to the push remote on an owner mismatch, an
37		// unparseable URL, or a protocol it cannot map. Reading settings directly
38		// would report "pinned" while pushes really went elsewhere, the same class
39		// of bug the CoreOrigin() rule in CLAUDE.md exists to prevent.
40		pinned bool
41	}
42	
43	// fansOut reports whether checkpoints pushed to this remote face more than one
44	// destination.
45	func (d remoteDestination) fansOut() bool { return !d.pinned && len(d.pushURLs) > 1 }

48	type remoteTopology struct {
49		// destinations is every configured remote, sorted by name.
50		destinations []remoteDestination
51		// primaryIsRefs reports whether the git-refs backend is active, which
52		// decides what a fanning-out remote means for checkpoints.
53		primaryIsRefs bool
54	}
55	
56	// inspectRemoteTopology reads the repo's remotes and checkpoint configuration.
57	// Best-effort and offline: every failure yields an empty topology, which reports
58	// nothing, because this is advisory output that must never obstruct enable or
59	// doctor.
60	func inspectRemoteTopology(ctx context.Context) remoteTopology {
61		var t remoteTopology
62	
63		repoRoot, err := paths.WorktreeRoot(ctx)
64		if err != nil {
65			return t
66		}
67	
68		// One `git remote -v` rather than `git remote` plus a get-url per remote:
69		// it already applies git's pushurl-replaces-url rule and lists every push
70		// URL in order, so N+1 subprocesses collapse to one — and all of it runs in
71		// repoRoot instead of mixing dir-aware and cwd-dependent lookups.
72		pushURLs, err := pushURLsByRemote(ctx, repoRoot)
73		if err != nil {
74			logging.Debug(ctx, "remote topology: could not read remotes", slog.String("error", err.Error()))
75			return t
76		}
77	
78		names := make([]string, 0, len(pushURLs))
79		for name := range pushURLs {
80			names = append(names, name)
81		}
82		sort.Strings(names)
83	
84		for _, name := range names {
85			dest := remoteDestination{name: name, pushURLs: pushURLs[name]}
86			if _, enabled, err := remote.PushURL(ctx, name); err == nil {
87				dest.pinned = enabled
88			}
89			t.destinations = append(t.destinations, dest)
90		}
91	
92		if cpCfg, err := settings.LoadCheckpointsConfig(ctx); err == nil {
93			t.primaryIsRefs = checkpoint.PrimaryIsRefs(cpCfg)
94		}
95	
96		return t
97	}
98	
99	// pushURLsByRemote parses `git remote -v` into remote name -> push URLs in git's
100	// own order.

content.text:
Correcting what I said before: `entire doctor` **does** check this — I was wrong that it doesn't. But what it prints is wrong, which is arguably worse.

## What doctor actually says

Repro: repo with `origin` + `fork`, `remote.pushDefault=fork`.

```
Checkpoint destination: REVIEW
  This repo has 2 remotes (fork, origin).
    Checkpoints follow whichever remote you push to, while reading them back
    (resume, explain) always looks at origin — so checkpoints pushed elsewhere
    are not found again from this clone.
  To pin one repository for checkpoints, set checkpoint_remote in
  .entire/settings.json (or .entire/settings.local.json to keep it to this clone).
```

Three problems:

**The first sentence is false.** "Checkpoints follow whichever remote you push to" is the pre-v0.10.0 behavior. Since the election change they follow only the elected remote — so in this repo they go to `origin` and the user's pushes to `fork` carry nothing. Doctor tells them the opposite of the actual failure. The stated hazard ("checkpoints pushed elsewhere are not found again") is now unreachable, because checkpoints can't be pushed elsewhere.

**It names the wrong setting.** The one-line fix is `strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote`. Doctor points at `checkpoint_remote` — a different feature (a dedicated metadata store addressed by URL). That does pin the destination and is exempt from the gate, so it's not useless advice, just a much heavier answer to the question the user has.

**It ignores the fix once applied.** With `checkpoint_push_remote: "fork"` set, `entire status` correctly reports `Checkpoints sync to: fork (set by checkpoint_push_remote)` — but doctor prints the identical `REVIEW` block and the identical wrong paragraph. `inspectRemoteTopology` (`remote_topology.go:60`) never reads that setting; `pinned` only asks about `checkpoint_remote` (`remote_topology.go:86`). So a correctly-configured repo is flagged forever.

## Why it's wrong

Two branches, same day, different files. The election change merged as PR #1893 (`caa0c9be9`, Aug 7); the destination note merged as `313463bcb` (Aug 7) from a branch that did **not** contain the election commit — `git merge-base --is-ancestor 3ef4422c5 a3136178c` → NO. Nothing conflicted, so git merged both cleanly and the prose was never reconciled against the new behavior.

The same wrong text also prints from `entire enable` (`setup.go:1382` and `setup.go:1393`), which is the moment the note was designed for — so new multi-remote users are mis-taught up front.

## So, to answer the original question

Intentional at the mechanism level; the user-facing story is broken. Their report is the predictable outcome: the one diagnostic that fires told them checkpoints follow their push.

The fix is small and worth doing in one pass:

1. Rewrite the `unpinnedNames()` paragraph in `describeCheckpointDestination` to state the election rule and name `checkpoint_push_remote`.
2. Teach `inspectRemoteTopology` about `checkpoint_push_remote` so a pinned repo stops being flagged.
3. Better: report the *actual* mismatch — compare the elected remote against the push destination git would use (`remote.pushDefault`, `branch.<name>.pushRemote`) and only warn when they differ. That's the condition that loses data, and it also catches the single-`origin`-plus-`pushDefault` case that `ambiguous()` reasoning gets to by accident.

Want me to do that? It's contained to `remote_topology.go` plus tests, and it's the difference between this being a docs bug and it staying a data-loss surprise.

result.output: 686:- **Single checkpoint sync remote** - checkpoint data syncs only to the elected checkpoint sync remote (`strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote` setting → `origin` → sole remote → first remote in `.git/config` order; fail-closed only when the setting names a missing remote), on both the git-branch and git-refs backends. The branch's tracking config (`branch.<name>.pushRemote`, `remote.pushDefault`, `branch.<name>.remote`) is deliberately **not** a tier: election is compared against the remote of the push being made, so electing the tracking remote silently drops checkpoint sync on every push to a different remote (`git push <other> HEAD`, a `git clone -o base` pushing checkpoints to a separately added `origin`, any repo with `remote.pushDefault`), and elects a remote the read paths — which resolve through origin's remote-tracking refs — cannot see. For a fork setup where `origin` is an unpushable base repo, name the fork with `checkpoint_push_remote`. Pushes to any other remote or to a raw URL never carry checkpoint data; the dedicated `checkpoint_remote` URL mode is exempt. `entire status` shows the sync destination and an unpushed-checkpoint count.

Done. Final state, verified end-to-end on a real repo:

**Before** (origin + fork, `remote.pushDefault=fork` — the reported setup):
```
Checkpoint destination: REVIEW
  This repo has 2 remotes (fork, origin).
    Checkpoints follow whichever remote you push to, ...   ← false since v0.10.0
  To pin one repository for checkpoints, set checkpoint_remote in ...   ← wrong setting
```

**After:**
```
Checkpoint destination: ACTION NEEDED
  Your pushes are NOT carrying checkpoints.
    `git push` goes to "fork", but checkpoints sync only to "origin" (the default),
    so a push to "fork" carries none.
    Fix: set "strategy_options": {"checkpoint_push_remote": "fork"} in
    .entire/settings.json (or .entire/settings.local.json for this clone only).
    Note: reading checkpoints back (resume, explain) looks at origin, so ones
    kept on "fork" are not found again from a fresh clone of origin.
```

## What changed

content.text:
Verified both. Short answer: yes, it's real — but the reporter's literal description isn't sufficient to cause it.

## It's real

With `remote.pushDefault=fork`, git itself confirms where the push goes:

```
$ git push -n -v
Pushing to ../fork.git
```

So the mismatch isn't synthetic. Election picks `origin`, git delivers to `fork`, the gate skips, nothing syncs.

One aside from that check: `git rev-parse main@{push}` returns `fatal: no upstream configured` in this exact state even though git pushes to `fork` happily. So `@{push}` is not a usable oracle here — which is why `resolveGitPushRemote` walks the tiers explicitly rather than asking git for the answer.

## But "my remote isn't called origin" alone is benign

If there's no `origin` at all, election falls to the sole-remote tier and syncs fine. The break needs `origin` (or a config-order-first remote) to exist *and* pushes to go elsewhere. So either the reporter has both, or they've concluded from `status` saying `origin` that nothing works when it actually does.

For a prevalence datapoint I scanned the repos on this machine: **31 repos, 29 single-`origin`, 2 with a second remote, 0 with `pushDefault` or `pushRemote` set** — zero mismatches locally. So this isn't the common shape; the reporter has a specific setup worth asking about.

## How you get there

1. **Git's triangular workflow** — the documented purpose of `remote.pushDefault`. Clone upstream as `origin`, add your fork, `git config remote.pushDefault fork`. First-class git feature, not exotic.
2. **`git clone -o base`** and adding `origin` later — already cited in the election code as the regression that killed the tracking tier.
3. **Gerrit / review remotes** — push to `gerrit`, `origin` is the read-only canonical.
4. **Corp read-only mirror as `origin`**, real pushes to a team remote.
5. **`branch.<name>.pushRemote` on one long-lived branch** — the nastiest variant, because sync breaks per-branch and looks intermittent.

Worth knowing what's *safe*: `gh repo fork` makes your fork `origin` and renames the original to `upstream` (per its own help text), so the most common fork flow elects your fork and works. Deploy remotes (`heroku`) are fine too — `pushDefault` stays `origin`, so only the deliberate `git push heroku` carries no checkpoints, which is correct. `gh repo fork --remote-name fork` *would* produce the broken shape.

## Detection

**One repo** — now `entire doctor`. There's also a pre-existing fingerprint nobody was reading: the unpushed-checkpoint counter in `entire status` climbs monotonically and **never drains**. A healthy repo's counter returns to zero after a push; this one only grows. That's the discriminating signature.

**Across the fleet — we currently can't, at all.** Telemetry sends one event, `cli_command_executed`, with command/agent/version/os/arch/flag *names*. Nothing about remotes. So we have no idea whether this is one person or a thousand; the report is our only evidence.

Server-side is weaker than it looks, and it's worth being clear why: if they never push to `origin`, our cell sees no commits *and* no checkpoints — indistinguishable from a dormant repo. The signal only exists for users who push to both.

So it has to be a client-side event, and there's already the right precedent: `checkpoint_policy_blocked` is fired from a gate structurally identical to this one (`emitCheckpointPolicyBlocked` — detached spawn, opt-in checked, no rate limit).

**The one design trap.** The obvious implementation — fire from `checkpointSyncAllowedForRemote` when it returns false — measures the wrong thing. That gate returns false for every raw-URL push and every deliberate push to a non-elected remote, so a `git push heroku` counts as a hit. You'd get a number dominated by intentional behavior. To measure *the bug*, compare election against the **default** push destination (what `resolveGitPushRemote` computes) and emit once per repo per day, not per push. Different signal, different call site.

Payload I'd send — no remote names or URLs, since a fork remote's name or URL identifies the user's org and CLAUDE.md restricts this to operational metadata:

```
event: checkpoint_sync_mismatch
  reason:            not_elected | election_failed
  sync_remote_source: config | default | sole | first
  push_dest_tier:     pushRemote | pushDefault | branchRemote | origin_fallback | unknown
  remote_count:       int
```

`push_dest_tier` is the field that actually decides the product question: if most hits come in via `pushDefault`, the setting is the wrong answer and election should follow the push destination after all — which is exactly the tier that got added and then reverted in `101b32853`/`74e239a9d`.

Want me to build that? It's ~1 file plus the daily-cadence stamp (the `version_check.json` pattern in the config dir is the existing precedent for once-a-day).

Good instinct — that's exactly what the checkpoint history is for. Let me find the session behind the revert.

fix(strategy): drop the tracking tier from checkpoint remote election

Electing the branch's push destination (branch.<name>.pushRemote ->
remote.pushDefault -> branch.<name>.remote) turned every push to a
different remote into a silent no-op, because the elected remote is
compared against the remote of the push actually being made. Any repo
where those differ lost checkpoint sync entirely: `git push <other>
HEAD`, a `git clone -o base` whose checkpoints go to a separately added
origin, anything with remote.pushDefault set.

TestAlternates_RelativeObjectAlternate_CheckpointSync caught it — it
clones with `-o base` and pushes checkpoints to `origin`, so the tracking
tier elected `base`, the gate rejected the `origin` push, and the pre-push
hook produced no output and synced nothing. That is the git-branch canary
failure on this PR; it passes with the tier removed.

The tier also elected a remote the read paths cannot see: resume and
explain resolve checkpoints through origin's remote-tracking refs, so
checkpoints routed to an implicitly elected non-origin remote could not
be read back from the same clone.

Precedence is now checkpoint_push_remote -> origin -> sole remote ->
first in .git/config order. The fork setup the tier was meant to serve
(origin is an unpushable base repo, you push to your own fork) is served
by naming the fork in checkpoint_push_remote, which is also the only
form of it where the checkpoints can be read back.

Tests: the three tracking-precedence unit tests collapse into
TestResolveCheckpointSyncRemote_TrackingConfigDoesNotDecide, a table
asserting each of the three git config keys leaves origin elected. The
dangling-tracking and detached-HEAD tests go with them — with no tracking
tier they assert the same thing. At integration level
ForkSetup_TracksNonOriginRemote inverts into
BranchTrackingDoesNotReroute. unsetBranchTracking existed only to defeat
the tier and is removed with its two call sites.

BODY: [https://entire.io/gh/entireio/cli/trails/967](<https://entire.io/gh/entireio/cli/trails/967>)

## Problem

In a repo with multiple remotes (e.g. `origin` and `publish`), pushing to **any** remote synced checkpoint data to it — leaking session transcripts onto remotes where they don't belong. The two storage backends failed in mirror-image ways:

* **git-branch**: every push re-synced `entire/checkpoints/v1`, so every remote received full transcripts (entireio/cli#1634, write side)
* **git-refs**: the push queue had no per-remote state, so the *first* push drained it and a second remote silently never received checkpoints (entireio/cli#1635)

## Change

Checkpoint data now syncs to exactly **one elected remote**, identical on both backends:

* **Election precedence** (`strategy.ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote`): `strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote` (a plain remote name; **fail-closed** — a name that isn't a configured remote disables sync with a warning rather than falling back) → **the current branch's own push destination**, mirroring git's push resolution (`branch.<name>.pushRemote` → `remote.pushDefault` → `branch.<name>.remote`; dangling tracking entries are skipped, not fail-closed) → `origin` → the sole remote → the first remote in `.git/config` order. The tracking tier fixes the fork setup where `origin` is a base repo the user cannot push (cloned base + added fork): the branch's tracking remote wins, so checkpoints sync to the fork instead of stranding locally.

The mechanism, from `alternates_test.go:100-109`: the fixture clones with the bare repo added as `origin` while the *work* repo's tracking config points at `base`. The tracking tier elected `base`, the hook was invoked as `pre-push origin`, the gate compared `base != origin` and returned `nil`. Checkpoints never moved.

## So the reason it was reverted

The tier was self-defeating, not merely risky. Election result is compared against the remote of the push *actually being made* — so electing the tracking remote makes every push to a different remote a silent no-op. It converts one narrow failure (fork setups stranding checkpoints locally) into a broad one (any repo where tracking ≠ push target syncs nothing), and the canary caught the broad case immediately.

Which means: **the tier cannot simply be reinstated** as the fix for the report we started from. If you want election to follow the push, election has to be evaluated per-push against the actual push remote rather than resolved once from config — a different design, not a reverted commit. ## Problem

On the git-refs backend, cross-machine **enumeration** never worked in the default setup: `ListCheckpointRefsOnRemote` returned nothing unless a dedicated `checkpoint_remote` was configured (scoped out when remote enumeration was introduced in #1771). A fresh clone running `checkpoint list` or the branch view saw zero checkpoints — even though known-ID hydration (`explain` on a commit with a trailer) worked fine. Repos with a dedicated store (like this one) never hit the gap, which is why it went unnoticed.

## Change

When no dedicated store is configured, discovery now ls-remotes the checkpoint read candidates — the elected sync remote (per #1893's election), then `origin` — for `refs/entire/checkpoints/*` and **merges the listings** (union, deduped): refs historically landed on whichever remote the pre-push hook fired for, so disjoint listings across remotes are realistic and first-non-empty would shadow one side. Known-ID hydration consumes the same election result: a fail-open `origin` read may satisfy a fetch, but an `origin` miss cannot falsely certify global absence when election failed.

- **Best-effort:** each candidate gets its own short budget, so a hung leader cannot starve the rest. Partial failure returns reachable results; total failure triggers the existing warning and degrades to a local-only listing.
- **Bounded hydration:** one chain-wide deadline covers all known-ID fetch candidates rather than granting each candidate a fresh full timeout.
- **Cheap:** ls-remote is names-only; runs only on enumeration paths that opt in (`WithRemoteListDiscovery`), never in hooks.
- **Token-aware:** candidate URLs resolve through `remote.FetchURL` with the new `LeadReadRemote` option, preserving the `ENTIRE_CHECKPOINT_TOKEN`-with-SSH-origin case.
- Dedicated `checkpoint_remote` behavior is byte-identical.

Looked at both now. Short version: **the report you brought me is already being fixed properly** — #1991 was opened at 02:09 today and quotes it verbatim as its motivation. That changes what my work should be.

## The stack, in merge order

| PR | What | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **#1956** | refs-native checkpoint discovery without a dedicated store; introduces `CheckpointReadRemotes` (elected remote → origin) | open, base of the stack |
| **#1951** | reads follow the elected remote, origin demoted to read-only legacy tier — metadata, policy, resume | open, stacked on #1956 (reconciled in `46fe95cd8`) |
| **#1991** | **capture**: pre-push persists the remote as the election when the push target agrees with the branch's declared destination | open, created today; says explicitly "merge after #1956 → #1951" |
| **#1987** | stderr hint on a gated pre-push when checkpoints are waiting (trail 1043) | open since last night |
| #1934 | `checkpoint_remote` ownership must be confirmed by the push destination | open, adjacent |

#1991's design is the right resolution of the thing we dug into yesterday. It requires the **intersection** of a declared push destination *and* an actual push to it — neither elects alone. Declaration alone is the config-at-rest bug that `74e239a9` reverted (pinned by a new `TestCheckpointSyncRemote_TrackingAloneDoesNotReroute`); a push alone is the pre-#1893 transcript leak. That's exactly the "election has to be per-push, not resolved once from config" conclusion, and they've built it.

## The one collision you'll want to arbitrate

**#1987 and #1991 edit the same lines** — `prePush` at `manual_commit_push.go:81-89`, plus both touch `checkpoint_sync_remote.go` and `checkpoint_sync_remote_test.go`. They'll conflict textually, but the bigger issue is that they're competing answers to the same moment:

- #1987 prints *"3 checkpoints are waiting to sync to "origin"… to sync to "fork" instead, set `checkpoint_push_remote`"*
- #1991 prints *"Checkpoints now sync to "fork" — the remote your branch pushes to"* and carries them on that same push

#1987 was written on the assumption that the tier was still an open product call — its body says so: *"whether election should gain a tracking tier … stays the product call deferred in #1893/#1951."* #1991 then answered it. So if #1991 lands, most of #1987's hint cases disappear into capture; the residual is a push to an **undeclared** remote (`git push other HEAD`), which capture deliberately won't act on. That residual is worth a hint — but it's a much narrower message than #1987 currently writes.

## Where my change stands

| Part | Verdict |

@@ -0,0 +1,72 @@
+package strategy
+
+import (
+	"context"
+	"log/slog"
+
+	"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/logging"
+)
+
+// CheckpointReadRemotes returns the ordered, deduped remotes that checkpoint
+// READS consult: the elected sync remote first, then "origin" as the legacy
+// tier (pre-single-remote-sync checkpoints live there, and a fresh clone
+// may lack the local settings that elected a non-origin remote).
+//
+// Unlike the write-side election, this fails OPEN: on an election error
+// (misconfigured checkpoint_push_remote, unreadable settings) the chain is
+// ["origin"] when configured. Writes fail closed to prevent leaking data;
+// failing reads closed would only prevent FINDING data, with no privacy
+// benefit. Callers must uphold the read-only rule for every candidate after
+// the first: only the elected remote may seed or advance local refs.
+//
+// An empty result means no candidates — callers needing the "checkpoint
+// absent" classification must gather their own positive evidence (successful
+// remote listing, readable settings); an empty chain alone is not proof.
+//
+// Deliberately un-memoized: every call re-runs the election (~2 git
+// subprocesses plus a settings.Load). Callers on hot paths (per-turn hooks,
+// checkpoint.Open sites) accept that cost for always-fresh results; revisit
+// with memoization only if profiling shows it matters.
+func CheckpointReadRemotes(ctx context.Context) []string {
+	return CheckpointReadRemotesWithElection(ctx).Candidates
+}
+
+// CheckpointReadResolution is the read-candidate chain bundled with the
+// election result it was derived from.
+type CheckpointReadResolution struct {
+	// Candidates is the ordered read-candidate chain (see
+	// CheckpointReadRemotes).
+	Candidates []string
+	// ElectedName is the elected checkpoint sync remote; "" when the election
+	// failed or elected nothing. Only this remote may seed or advance local
+	// refs.
+	ElectedName string
+	// ElectionErr records a failed election. It is advisory for readers (the
+	// chain fail-opens to ["origin"] when configured); write-adjacent callers
+	// may surface it when they need a push target.
+	ElectionErr error
+}
+
+// CheckpointReadRemotesWithElection returns the read-candidate chain together
+// with the election result it was derived from, so callers that need both —
+// e.g. to confine local-ref advancement to the elected remote while iterating
+// the chain — make ONE election call instead of two that could disagree if
+// settings or remotes change mid-operation. See CheckpointReadRemotes for the
+// read-side fail-open rationale and cost note.
+func CheckpointReadRemotesWithElection(ctx context.Context) CheckpointReadResolution {
+	var res CheckpointReadResolution
+	elected, err := ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote(ctx)
+	switch {
+	case err != nil:
+		res.ElectionErr = err
+		logging.Debug(ctx, "checkpoint reads: election failed, falling back to origin only",
+			slog.String("error", err.Error()))
+	case elected.Name != "":
+		res.ElectedName = elected.Name
+		res.Candidates = append(res.Candidates, elected.Name)
+	}
+	if isConfiguredRemote(ctx, "origin") && (len(res.Candidates) == 0 || res.Candidates[0] != "origin") {
+		res.Candidates = append(res.Candidates, "origin")
+	}
+	return res
+}

+// hintGatedCheckpointSync tells the user, on a gated pre-push, that
+// checkpoints are waiting for the elected sync remote and how to re-route
+// them — otherwise the gate is a silent no-op and checkpoints strand locally
+// until the elected remote happens to be pushed.
+//
+// Stays quiet unless every condition holds: the push target is a configured
+// remote (checkpoint_push_remote takes a remote name, so a raw-URL push has
+// no actionable suggestion), the election succeeded AND was automatic (an
+// explicit checkpoint_push_remote is a decision already made, and the
+// fail-closed misconfigured case logs a warning through the gate itself), and
+// checkpoints are actually waiting. Fully local — no network.
+//
+// The hint names .entire/settings.local.json: a remote name is a per-clone
+// fact, and committing it to the tracked settings.json would fail-close
+// checkpoint sync for every teammate whose clone lacks that remote name.
+func hintGatedCheckpointSync(ctx context.Context, pushRemote string) {
+	if !isConfiguredRemote(ctx, pushRemote) {
+		return
+	}
+	syncRemote, err := ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote(ctx)
+	if err != nil || syncRemote.Name == "" || syncRemote.Source == SyncRemoteSourceConfig {
+		return
+	}
+	count, err := CountUnpushedCheckpoints(ctx, syncRemote.Name)
+	if err != nil {
+		// Stay quiet toward the user (best-effort hint in their push), but
+		// leave a trace: a persistently failing count would otherwise
+		// re-create the silent stall this hint exists to surface.
+		logging.Debug(ctx, "gated checkpoint sync hint suppressed: cannot count unpushed checkpoints",
+			slog.String("checkpoint_sync_remote", syncRemote.Name),
+			slog.String("error", err.Error()))
+		return
+	}
+	if count == 0 {
+		return
+	}
+	fmt.Fprintf(stderrWriter,
+		"[entire] %d checkpoint(s) are waiting to sync to %q, this repo's checkpoint sync remote; this push to %q does not carry them.\n",
+		count, syncRemote.Name, pushRemote)
+	fmt.Fprintf(stderrWriter,
+		"[entire] To sync checkpoints to %q instead, set strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote to %q in .entire/settings.local.json.\n",
+		pushRemote, pushRemote)
+	logging.Info(ctx, "gated checkpoint sync hint shown",
+		slog.Int("unpushed_checkpoints", count),
+		slog.String("checkpoint_sync_remote", syncRemote.Name),
+		slog.String("push_remote", pushRemote))
+}

content.text:
Reviewed all four. The designs are good — #1991 in particular is the right resolution of the tier question. Six findings, one of which I'd fix before merge.

## Blocker

**#1987 — the hint fires on intentional pushes, and the advice is harmful.** `hintGatedCheckpointSync` gates on three things: configured remote, automatic election, checkpoints waiting. It never asks whether the pushed remote is one the user *habitually* pushes. Verified end-to-end on the branch — repo with `origin` + a `heroku` deploy remote, one waiting checkpoint:

```
$ entire hooks git pre-push heroku
[entire] 1 checkpoint(s) are waiting to sync to "origin", … this push to "heroku" does not carry them.
[entire] To sync checkpoints to "heroku" instead, set strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote to "heroku" …
```

Following that advice routes session transcripts to a deploy remote. Same output for a one-off `git push upstream` on someone else's repo — which is precisely the transcript leak #1893 existed to stop, and which #1991's body names as the reason capture requires declaration. And since a gated push never drains the queue, the count only grows, so it nags on every deploy forever.

Fix is one condition: also require `declaredPushDestination(ctx) == pushRemote` — the helper #1991 adds. Then the three cases separate cleanly:

| Situation | Behavior |
|---|---|
| declared == pushed, nothing captured yet | #1991 captures + announces |
| declared == pushed, capture already spent | #1987 hints — advice is correct |
| declared != pushed (deploy, one-off PR) | **silent** |

`TestHintGatedCheckpointSync` has four subtests and none covers the third row.

## Worth fixing, not blocking

**#1991 — capture state is unlocked with a fixed temp path.** Its own comment cites the push queue as precedent ("git common dir, worktree-shared, like the push queue"), but `pushqueue.go` is flock-protected through the existing `internal/flock` package. `saveCapturedSyncRemotes` uses a shared `path + ".tmp"` and the load→save sequence isn't atomic. Two worktrees pushing concurrently can both see "nothing captured" and both write, or interleave on the shared tmp file so the announced remote isn't the persisted one — and first-capture-sticks makes that stick. `flock.Acquire` + `os.CreateTemp` in the same dir.

**#1951 — per-candidate fetch timeout, against #1956's own principle.** `fetchMetadataFromRemote` grants each candidate a fresh `2*time.Minute`; #1956 deliberately uses a chain-wide `readFetchTimeout` for the analogous chain and says so ("bounds the complete chain, not each candidate"). A hung legacy origin doubles resume latency to four minutes. Same family, opposite policy — worth unifying on the chain-wide form. Related: it fetches every candidate with no early exit (justified in the comment), which doubles network for multi-remote users on every metadata fetch.

**#1991 — 2–3 elections per pre-push.** `maybeCapture` resolves, then `checkpointSyncAllowedForRemote` resolves again; with #1987 the gated path makes three. Each is ~2 subprocesses plus `settings.Load`, and the resolver documents itself as deliberately un-memoized. Pre-push is the one caller where threading the resolution through would pay.

## Correct as built

- **#1956's resolver** — fail-open for reads with the rationale stated (failing reads closed prevents finding data with no privacy benefit), the confinement rule documented as a caller obligation, and `CheckpointReadRemotesWithElection` exists specifically so chain and election can't disagree. Layering is right: capture lands in `ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote`, so the read chain picks it up for free.
- **#1951's confinement** — `advanceLocal` is `ElectedName != "" && remoteName == ElectedName`, gating `SafelyAdvanceLocalRef` so a stale origin can't rebase local v1. The doctor change extends the same rule to the repair path and degrades to report-only. That's the #1374 hazard properly contained.
- **#1991's capture** — intersection of declaration and behavior, fail-soft captured tier vs fail-closed explicit setting, list-shaped state from day one, and `TestCheckpointSyncRemote_TrackingAloneDoesNotReroute` pins the `74e239a9` regression. In my deploy-remote repro capture correctly did nothing (no declaration), so it does not introduce the #1987 problem.

## Merge order

1. **#1956** — self-contained, no dependencies
2. **#1951** — needs #1956 (divergence reconciled in `46fe95cd8`)
3. **#1991** — needs the read stack; merging it earlier routes checkpoints to a remote pre-#1951 reads can't see. Its body already states this
4. **#1987** — last, absorbing the declaration check so it can use `declaredPushDestination`

#1987 and #1991 conflict textually at `manual_commit_push.go:81-89`. Merged form:

```go
if !ps.hasCheckpointURL() {
    maybeCaptureCheckpointSyncRemote(ctx, ps.remote)
    if !checkpointSyncAllowedForRemote(ctx, ps.remote) {
        hintGatedCheckpointSync(ctx, ps.remote)
        return nil
    }
}
```

They also both add cases to `checkpoint_sync_remote_test.go` and the integration file — mechanical.

## My uncommitted work

One more overlap worth naming: #1991's `declaredPushDestination` and my `resolveGitPushRemote` are the same logic twice (mine additionally falls through to `origin`, git's final tier, which theirs deliberately omits). Two implementations of git's precedence is exactly what produced the stale-prose bug in the first place. Mine should consume theirs once #1991 lands.

So my plan stands as described: ship the wording/misfire fix now (true under both old and new behavior, drops the CLAUDE.md hunk and the read-path caveat), and rebase the mismatch detection behind #1991.

Description:
Problem:
Checkpoint refs discovery required a dedicated checkpoint_remote configuration to find checkpoints written on another machine. Without this setting, a fresh clone on a second machine showed no checkpoints in checkpoint list, even though they existed on the remote, because discovery was restricted to the configured remote only.
Solution:
The change implements automatic multi-remote checkpoint discovery when no dedicated checkpoint_remote is configured. Instead of querying only one target, the code now:
Queries multiple "read candidate" remotes in order: the elected checkpoint sync remote first, then "origin" as a legacy tier
Merges checkpoint ref listings from all candidates into a union deduped by ref name, so refs scattered across remotes are all discovered
Makes discovery best-effort: if one remote fails to respond, others are still queried; if all fail, discovery returns nothing without error
Preserves the existing single-target behavior when a checkpoint_remote is explicitly configured
This closes the gap in the default setup. Users on a second machine now discover refs-native checkpoints on their elected sync remote or origin without needing to configure a separate checkpoint_remote, while the explicit configuration path remains unchanged.

content.text:
Two of the three premises don't hold, but the third one lands — and it's a real gap.

## "All heads" — it isn't

`branchName := refs.Primary.Short()`, which is `entire/checkpoints/v1`. The refspec names one exact branch. There are no wildcard fetch refspecs anywhere in the CLI (grepped `refs/heads/*`, `:refs/remotes/*` → nothing), and only **two** force refspecs in the entire codebase, both this same metadata-branch pattern in `git_operations.go:318` and `:408`. #1951 changes only the middle `%s` from a hardcoded `origin` to the candidate name — the source side stays one named branch.

## "Could override things from the user" — not at this layer

The destination is `refs/remotes/<remote>/entire/checkpoints/v1` — a **remote-tracking** ref. Nothing the user authored lives there; it's a cache of remote state. Both force refspecs write only to `refs/remotes/...`; neither touches a local branch or the working tree.

And the `+` is *less* forceful than git's own default: a stock `git remote add` writes `fetch = +refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*` — forced, and wildcarded. So this is the normal way to maintain a tracking ref, narrowed to one branch.

## Why the force is load-bearing

Dropping it would break things rather than protect anything. `entire/checkpoints/v1` diverges non-fast-forward by design: the OPF pre-push rewrite rebuilds commits with an `Entire-OPF-Applied` trailer and CAS-updates the ref; condensation and the disconnected-metadata repair cherry-pick onto a new tip. Without `+`, fetching a diverged v1 into the tracking ref **fails outright** — so `IsMetadataDisconnected` and `entire doctor`'s repair could never observe the remote tip they exist to reconcile against. The `+` is what lets us *see* remote reality; it doesn't decide what to do about it.

That decision lives in `SafelyAdvanceLocalRef` (`strategy/common.go:158`), the only thing that moves the local ref, and it does earn its name:

| Case | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `mergeBase == targetHash` (local ahead) | **no-op** — won't rewind you |
| `mergeBase == localHash` | fast-forward |
| diverged | `replayLocalRefFromBase` — replays your local commits onto the fetched tip |
| no merge base | `replayDisconnectedLocalRef`; if shallow history prevents *proving* disconnection it **errors** and points at doctor rather than guessing |

No path discards local commits. So the force fetch can't silently lose checkpoints.

## Where your instinct is right

**The replay is completely silent.** Zero logging calls across the whole chain — `SafelyAdvanceLocalRef`, `replayLocalRefFromBase`, `replayDisconnectedLocalRef`, `replayLocalCommits`, `setRefHash`. So when a fetch discovers divergence and the CLI rewrites your local v1 by replaying your commits onto a remote tip, nothing is written to the log, let alone to the user. That's a local-ref rewrite with no trace — exactly the "without them noticing" you're pointing at, just one layer down from the refspec. It's also pre-existing, not introduced by #1951.

**#1951 and #1991 widen it.** Pre-#1951, only `origin` could drive that advance. #1951 confines it to the *elected* remote (verified: `advanceLocal` is gated on `remoteName == resolution.ElectedName`) — correct in itself. But with #1991's capture, the elected remote can now change **automatically** from an observed push. So the set of remotes permitted to rewrite your local v1 stops being fixed by config and starts growing by behavior. Capture announces itself, so it isn't hidden — but the consequence ("this remote may now replay your local checkpoint history") isn't stated anywhere.

Two things I'd suggest, neither blocking the stack:

1. `logging.Info` in the two replay paths recording ref, local tip, target tip, and commits replayed. Cheap, and it makes an invisible rewrite forensically visible in `.entire/logs/` — which matters because this is the `#1374`-class hazard the confinement comment already worries about.
2. A doctor line when local v1 and the elected remote's tracking ref have diverged, since `IsMetadataDisconnected` already computes exactly that and doctor already reports the disconnected case. Divergence-with-replay currently passes silently.

// writeMetadataCommitWithParent builds a metadata commit on top of parent, so a
// test can construct genuinely diverged history (shared base, two children)
// rather than the rootless commits the disconnection tests use.
func writeMetadataCommitWithParent(t *testing.T, repo *git.Repository, message string, parent plumbing.Hash) plumbing.Hash {
	t.Helper()
	emptyTree := &object.Tree{Entries: []object.TreeEntry{}}
	treeObj := repo.Storer.NewEncodedObject()
	require.NoError(t, emptyTree.Encode(treeObj))
	treeHash, err := repo.Storer.SetEncodedObject(treeObj)
	require.NoError(t, err)

	commitObj := &object.Commit{
		Author:       object.Signature{Name: "test", Email: "test@test.com", When: time.Now()},
		Committer:    object.Signature{Name: "test", Email: "test@test.com", When: time.Now()},
		Message:      message,
		TreeHash:     treeHash,
		ParentHashes: []plumbing.Hash{parent},
	}
	enc := repo.Storer.NewEncodedObject()
	require.NoError(t, commitObj.Encode(enc))
	hash, err := repo.Storer.SetEncodedObject(enc)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	return hash
}

// setupDivergedMetadata points local v1 and origin's tracking ref at two
// different children of one base commit, and returns both tips.
func setupDivergedMetadata(t *testing.T, repo *git.Repository) (local, remote plumbing.Hash) {
	t.Helper()
	base := writeRootlessMetadataCommit(t, repo, "shared base")
	local = writeMetadataCommitWithParent(t, repo, "local checkpoint", base)
	remote = writeMetadataCommitWithParent(t, repo, "remote checkpoint", base)

	require.NoError(t, repo.Storer.SetReference(plumbing.NewHashReference(
		plumbing.NewBranchReferenceName(paths.MetadataBranchName), local)))
	require.NoError(t, repo.Storer.SetReference(plumbing.NewHashReference(
		plumbing.NewRemoteReferenceName("origin", paths.MetadataBranchName), remote)))
	return local, remote
}

	t.Helper()
	cmd := &cobra.Command{}

	cmd.SetErr(&stderr)
	require.NoError(t, checkDisconnectedMetadata(cmd, true))

}

// that previously printed a bare "OK": local and remote both advanced, so the

func TestCheckDisconnectedMetadata_Diverged_ReportedAsSelfHealing(t *testing.T) {
	// Cannot use t.Parallel(): t.Chdir and IsolateGitConfigEnv modify globals.
	testutil.IsolateGitConfigEnv(t)
	dir := setupGitRepoForPhaseTest(t)

	repo, err := git.PlainOpen(dir)

	local, remote := setupDivergedMetadata(t, repo)

	// origin is the elected remote here, so the replay really will happen.
	testutil.AddRemote(t, dir, "origin", "https://example.com/origin.git")

	output := runCheckDisconnectedMetadata(t)

	assert.Contains(t, output, "Metadata branches: DIVERGED")
	assert.NotContains(t, output, "DISCONNECTED", "shared ancestry is not a disconnection")
	assert.Contains(t, output, local.String()[:12], "the local tip must be shown")
	assert.Contains(t, output, remote.String()[:12], "the remote tip must be shown")
	assert.Contains(t, output, "No action needed", "divergence against the elected remote self-heals")
	assert.Contains(t, output, "new hashes", "the user must learn the replayed commits are re-hashed")

	localRef, err := repo.Reference(plumbing.NewBranchReferenceName(paths.MetadataBranchName), true)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	assert.Equal(t, local, localRef.Hash(), "reporting must not move any ref")
}

// TestCheckDisconnectedMetadata_Diverged_LegacyTierWontReconcile is the other
// half: the confinement rule means a diverged legacy-tier ref never advances the
// local ref, so promising self-healing there would be a lie.
func TestCheckDisconnectedMetadata_Diverged_LegacyTierWontReconcile(t *testing.T) {
	testutil.IsolateGitConfigEnv(t)
	dir := setupGitRepoForPhaseTest(t)
	t.Chdir(dir)

	repo, err := git.PlainOpen(dir)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	setupDivergedMetadata(t, repo)

	// Election picks upstream; origin carries the diverged tracking ref.
	testutil.AddRemote(t, dir, "origin", "https://example.com/origin.git")
	testutil.AddRemote(t, dir, "upstream", "https://example.com/upstream.git")
	testutil.WriteCheckpointPushRemoteSetting(t, dir, "upstream")

	output := runCheckDisconnectedMetadata(t)

	assert.Contains(t, output, "Metadata branches: DIVERGED")
	assert.Contains(t, output, "legacy read tier")
	assert.Contains(t, output, "Nothing will reconcile this on its own.")
	assert.NotContains(t, output, "No action needed",
		"a legacy-tier divergence does not self-heal; saying so would be wrong")
}

// TestCheckDisconnectedMetadata_Aligned_StaysQuiet pins that the common case is
// unchanged — the divergence check must not add noise to a healthy repo.
func TestCheckDisconnectedMetadata_Aligned_StaysQuiet(t *testing.T) {
	testutil.IsolateGitConfigEnv(t)
	dir := setupGitRepoForPhaseTest(t)
	t.Chdir(dir)

	repo, err := git.PlainOpen(dir)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	tip := writeRootlessMetadataCommit(t, repo, "agreed metadata")
	require.NoError(t, repo.Storer.SetReference(plumbing.NewHashReference(
		plumbing.NewBranchReferenceName(paths.MetadataBranchName), tip)))
	require.NoError(t, repo.Storer.SetReference(plumbing.NewHashReference(
		plumbing.NewRemoteReferenceName("origin", paths.MetadataBranchName), tip)))
	testutil.AddRemote(t, dir, "origin", "https://example.com/origin.git")

	output := runCheckDisconnectedMetadata(t)

	assert.Contains(t, output, "✓ Metadata branches: OK")
	assert.NotContains(t, output, "DIVERGED")
}

// fetch reaches past remote-tracking refs and rewrites local state. The whole
// advance/replay chain used to be silent, which made an after-the-fact
// investigation impossible: the ref had moved, the local commits had new hashes,
// and .entire/logs/ said nothing about it.
//
// Not parallel: t.Chdir plus the process-global logger.
func TestSafelyAdvanceLocalRef_LogsTheReplay(t *testing.T) {
	cloneDir, run := divergenceRepo(t)

	run("checkout", paths.MetadataBranchName)
	base := gitOut(t, cloneDir, "rev-parse", "HEAD")
	commitOnMetadataBranch(t, cloneDir, run, filepath.Join("aa", "6666666666"), `{"side":"local"}`)
	localTip := gitOut(t, cloneDir, "rev-parse", "HEAD")
	run("checkout", "-b", "remote-side", base)
	commitOnMetadataBranch(t, cloneDir, run, filepath.Join("bb", "7777777777"), `{"side":"remote"}`)
	remoteTip := gitOut(t, cloneDir, "rev-parse", "HEAD")
	run("update-ref", "refs/heads/"+paths.MetadataBranchName, localTip)
	run("checkout", "main")

	repo, err := git.PlainOpen(cloneDir)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	localRefName := plumbing.NewBranchReferenceName(paths.MetadataBranchName)
	require.NoError(t, SafelyAdvanceLocalRef(t.Context(), repo, localRefName, plumbing.NewHash(remoteTip)))
	logging.Close() // flush the buffered writer

	data, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(cloneDir, ".entire", "logs", "entire.log"))
	require.NoError(t, err)
	logged := string(data)

	assert.Contains(t, logged, "local ref will be rewritten", "the rewrite must be announced in the log")
	assert.Contains(t, logged, "diverged", "the reason must distinguish diverged from disconnected")
	assert.Contains(t, logged, localTip, "the pre-rewrite local tip must be recoverable from the log")
	assert.Contains(t, logged, remoteTip, "the target tip must be recorded")
	assert.Contains(t, logged, "commits_replayed", "the replayed-commit count must be recorded")

	// The replay itself must still preserve the local checkpoint.
	after, err := repo.Reference(localRefName, true)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	assert.NotEqual(t, plumbing.NewHash(remoteTip), after.Hash(),
		"the local commit is replayed on top, so the ref is not merely reset to the remote tip")
}

## Item 1 — the replay leaves a trace

`logLocalRefReplay` in `strategy/common.go`, called from both `replayLocalRefFromBase` and `replayDisconnectedLocalRef`, recording ref, pre-rewrite local tip, target tip, replayed-commit count, and a `diverged`/`disconnected` reason. `Info` rather than `Debug` — the default level has to carry it or a post-hoc investigation won't find it. Metadata only, per the logging privacy rule.

`TestSafelyAdvanceLocalRef_LogsTheReplay` asserts against the real `.entire/logs/entire.log` after driving an actual replay, so it pins the content, not just that a call exists.

## Item 2 — doctor reports divergence

New `strategy.MetadataDivergenceFromRemote` classifies local vs a remote-tracking ref; `entire doctor` now prints this instead of a bare `OK`. Real output:

```
Metadata branches: DIVERGED
  Local and remote entire/checkpoints/v1 have both advanced since they last agreed.
    local:  8415df1ee184
    remote: 7c46565c7e7c  (origin)
  No action needed: the next fetch from this remote replays your local
  checkpoints onto its tip. No checkpoints are lost, but the local ref moves
  and the replayed commits get new hashes.
```

And when the diverged ref is the legacy tier, the promise would be false, so it says the opposite:

```
  "origin" is the legacy read tier, not the elected checkpoint sync remote, so it
  never advances the local ref. Nothing will reconcile this on its own.
```

That distinction falls straight out of #1951's confinement rule — which is why this belongs on that branch rather than main.

The classifier stays disjoint from `IsMetadataDisconnected`: no-merge-base reports `false` here and keeps its existing DISCONNECTED report plus repair. Ahead/behind in either direction is a fast-forward and stays quiet, so healthy repos see no new output.

## Verification

`go build`, `go vet`, `mise run lint` (0 issues), `mise run test:ci` green — Vogon 56/56, roger-roger 4/4. 10 new tests: 6 classifier states, the log assertion, 3 doctor outputs.

One thing worth flagging: my first full `test:ci` had two failures in `cmd/entire/cli/agent/external` (`TestDiscoverAndRegisterNamedAlways_InvalidInfo`, `TestDiscoverAndRegister_ContinuesAfterRegistrationError`), both at exactly 10.0s. That's `discoveryTimeout = 10 * time.Second` in `discovery.go:27` — subprocess-spawning tests hitting a hardcoded timeout on a saturated machine. They pass in 0.6s in isolation, a clean re-run of the full suite was green, and I touch nothing in that package. Load-sensitive flake, pre-existing, but it will bite CI occasionally.

## One decision left

The branch is pushed but I haven't opened a PR, because the base choice affects your merge train and I'd rather you pick:

- **Stacked PR** targeting `fix/checkpoint-read-remotes` — keeps #1951 the size the reviewers already have, and GitHub auto-retargets to main once #1951 merges. My recommendation, since #1951 is on the critical path to #1991.
- **Fold into #1951** — one fewer PR, but grows an unapproved 43-file PR that's blocking the fix for your original report. `git cherry-pick 46ae87d88` onto that branch.

Say which and I'll do it. The worktree is still set up either way.

[4:07 PM]Some additional pointers from Claude:
- Perf: CheckpointReadRemotes is un-memoized (~2 git subprocesses + settings.Load) and called at nearly every checkpoint.Open, including per-turn hooks — a documented tradeoff worth watching.
- Perf: Per-candidate timeouts (commit 08, a real fix) multiply worst-case latency — blob hydration is now 2m per target and the old whole-function cap is gone; a fully-stalled read can hang notably longer.

Confirmed un-memoized by design (the doc comment says so explicitly). ~30 non-test call sites, and it *is* on the per-turn path: `getEphemeralStore` → `getCheckpointStores` → `CheckpointReadRemotes`, which the shadow-branch write path calls on SaveStep, plus `finalizeAllTurnCheckpoints` at Stop.

Measured with a PATH-shimmed `git` counting subprocesses, same repo, one remote, `entire checkpoint list`:

| | total git subprocesses | election-shaped |
|---|---|---|
| `origin/main` | **9** | 3 |
| #1951 | **15** | 9 |

So +67% total, and election resolution itself tripled. Per election it's one `config --local --get-regexp ^remote\..*\.url$` plus one-or-more `remote get-url <name>` (that's `isConfiguredRemote`, `manual_commit_push.go:240`), plus a `settings.Load` file read. Four elections ran for that one command.

Two things sharpen it beyond "worth watching":

- **#1991 adds to each election** — `loadCapturedSyncRemotes` puts another file read in the same path, so the cost grows again when capture lands.
- **This repo already treats per-hook git cost as a known hazard** — CLAUDE.md's `gitrepo.Status` rule exists because one status walk per hook was too much, and it explicitly documents that the turn-start hook walking twice is a known wart. Adding 3× election resolution to the same hooks runs against that grain.

Mitigating: these are all local, no network, so absolute cost on a warm FS is small. This reads as a solid follow-up, not a merge blocker. The fix is easy in shape (thread one `CheckpointReadResolution` through, which `CheckpointReadRemotesWithElection` was already built for) but touches many call sites.

## Claim 2 — per-candidate timeouts: relevant, and it's three paths, not one

The claim understates it. #1951 flips **three** read paths from a single cap to per-candidate, and one of them reverses a decision #1956 made deliberately days earlier in the same stack:

**1. Ref hydration — a direct reversal.** On main (post-#1956):

```go
chainCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, readFetchTimeout)   // outside the loop
// "The readFetchTimeout bounds the complete chain, not each candidate."
```

On #1951, `WithTimeout` moved *inside* the `for i, remoteName := range readRemotes` loop, and the constant's comment was rewritten from "bounds one complete interactive read-chain attempt" to "bounds each interactive read-candidate attempt". So it's an intentional change with the comment updated to match — but it undoes #1956's explicit choice, and that comment was load-bearing precisely to prevent this.

**2. Blob hydration — the whole-function cap is gone, as claimed.** Main wrapped the entire function:

```go
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 2*time.Minute)
defer cancel()
```

That derived ctx covered the fetch *and* both fallbacks. #1951 applies 2m per target in a loop, then runs `FetchMetadataFromCheckpointRemote` / `FetchMetadataBranch` on the **original uncapped** ctx.

**3. Metadata branch** — 2m per candidate in `fetchMetadataFromReadRemotes`, was a single 2m for origin.

And they nest. One blob-hydration miss: 2m × targets, then the fallback into `FetchMetadataBranch` → 2m × candidates. With two candidates (elected + origin) that's **~8 minutes worst case against main's 2**.

**No outer cap exists.** `main.go` uses `context.WithCancel`, not `WithTimeout`. `resume.go` has zero timeouts. The only caps are on explain's list-hydration pass (`ListHydrationTimeout` 15s, `ListHydrationPassTimeout` 30s), which don't cover resume or the general read paths. So nothing bounds this above.

## My read

Claim 2 deserves a decision before merge, not because it's wrong-by-design — per-candidate budgets are defensible, a stalled leader shouldn't consume the follower's window — but because the stack now contains both policies with no stated rationale for the split, and the interactive worst case quadrupled on `entire resume`, which has no other cap. Cheapest resolution: keep per-candidate budgets but add a chain-wide ceiling (`fetchBlobsByHash` covering its fallbacks again), so a fully-stalled read is bounded by one number rather than N × 2m.

git -c user.name="Stefan Haubold" -c user.email="stefan@entire.io" commit -q -F - <<'MSG'
perf(checkpoint): bound the read chain and stop re-electing per call

Two costs the read-candidate chain introduced, both measured against
origin/main with a PATH-shimmed git counting subprocesses.

Unbounded worst case. Per-candidate budgets replaced single shared ones —
a real fix, since one shared budget let a hung leader starve the legacy
origin tier — but nothing bounded the total, and these read paths have no
outer deadline: `entire resume` sets none and main() uses
context.WithCancel, not WithTimeout. fetchBlobsByHash lost the most: it
used to run inside one 2-minute budget that also covered its fallback
fetches, and per-target budgets left those fallbacks on the caller's
uncapped context, so a stalled hydration could spend per-target budgets
and then a fresh per-candidate metadata chain on top.

ReadChainBudget (2x readFetchTimeout) now wraps all three chains —
checkpoint ref hydration, the metadata branch chain, and blob hydration
including its fallbacks — with per-candidate budgets nested inside. Both
properties hold: every candidate still gets its own window, and the total
stall stays bounded. Injectable on the private helpers alongside the
existing fetchTimeout parameter so the ceiling is testable in
milliseconds.

Election cost per command. The election re-runs on every call by design,
and each run shells out to git twice over .git/config: which remotes
exist, and does remote X exist. One command elects several times —
`entire checkpoint list` resolves the chain four times (disconnection
warning, branch listing, the git-refs store's remote discovery, imported
rewind points), spending 15 git subprocesses where main spent 9.

WithGitRemoteCache memoizes only those two .git/config reads for one
invocation, installed once in main(). The election result, settings, and

Both fixed and pushed as `soph/checkpoint-read-budget` (`d2b031972`), branched off #1951.

## Fix 2 — bounded read chains

`ReadChainBudget` (2× `readFetchTimeout`) now wraps all three chains, with per-candidate budgets nested inside, so both properties hold: a hung candidate burns only its own window (what #1951 was fixing), and the total stall is bounded (what main had).

- `fetchCheckpointRefFrom` — ref hydration
- `fetchMetadataFromReadRemotes` — metadata branch
- `fetchBlobsByHash` — the worst one, where the ceiling now covers the fallback fetches again, not just the loop

Made injectable next to the existing `fetchTimeout` param so it's testable in milliseconds. The test stalls every target and asserts the call returns in ~ceiling rather than per-target × targets. I verified it's a real guard by disabling the ceiling: **0.33s with it, 5.19s and failing without.**

## Fix 1 — election cost, fully recovered

`WithGitRemoteCache` memoizes only the two `.git/config` reads (which remotes exist; does remote X exist), installed once in `main()`.

Design points that matter:

- **The election result is not cached.** Settings and the captured-election file stay uncached, so a write→re-resolve still sees the new value — **#1991's capture keeps working**, which a naive election cache would have silently broken.
- **Context-scoped and opt-in**, so an uninstrumented context behaves exactly as today. Tests pass plain contexts → uncached path → no risk of one temp repo's remote list leaking into another. That sidesteps the hazard behind CLAUDE.md's warning about the reverted `Status` memoization.
- **`repo mirror use`** is the CLI's only git-remote mutation, and it invalidates.
- **`WarnIfMetadataDisconnected` now takes a ctx** instead of building `context.Background()`. That detached context ignored *interrupt cancellation* as well as the cache — a real bug beyond the perf issue, since Ctrl-C couldn't interrupt its git probe.

Measured, `entire checkpoint list`, PATH-shimmed git:

| | git subprocesses | `get-regexp` | `remote get-url` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `origin/main` | 9 | 1 | 2 |
| #1951 (parent) | 15 | 4 | 5 |
| **+ these fixes** | **9** | **1** | **2** |

Regression fully recovered, not just reduced.

## Verification

`mise run fmt`, `mise run lint` (0 issues), `mise run test:ci` — all packages ok, Vogon 56/56, roger-roger 4/4.

One process note: partway through I ran `git checkout --` on `git_operations.go` to undo a temporary experiment and wiped all three of that file's edits along with it. I re-applied them and re-confirmed the 9-subprocess measurement and the ceiling test afterward, so the pushed tree is verified — but worth knowing the intermediate state existed.

## Two branches now waiting on you

Both off `fix/checkpoint-read-remotes`, independent of each other:

- `soph/checkpoint-replay-visibility` (`46ae87d88`) — the replay logging + doctor DIVERGED
- `soph/checkpoint-read-budget` (`d2b031972`) — these two perf/latency fixes

I still haven't opened PRs for either, since the base choice is yours. My recommendation is unchanged: stack both on `fix/checkpoint-read-remotes` so GitHub auto-retargets to main when #1951 lands. The budget one has a stronger case for folding directly into #1951 though — it fixes regressions that PR introduces, so a reviewer would reasonably expect them in the same change. Say which and I'll open them.

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are

include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,

### Efficiency

content.text:
Both measurements hold: election cost still at main's baseline of 9, and doctor's `merge-base` calls went **2 → 1**. All three sets lint clean with full `test:ci` green.

## Fixed

**The one that mattered — my ceiling was decorative.** `ReadChainBudget` was `2 × readFetchTimeout`, exactly the 2-candidate worst case, so it could never bind and blob hydration's fallbacks inherited an expired context. Now an absolute `3 * time.Minute` (binds for any chain of ≥2, leaves a single-candidate chain untouched, doesn't silently go wrong when a third tier appears), plus `ReadChainLoopBudget` reserving a sixth of the ceiling so the fallbacks are *funded* rather than merely inside it. Exported `ReadFetchTimeout` and removed the two bare `2*time.Minute` literals that had to stay silently equal to it. Reshaped the test to production ratios — it now requires ≥2 targets and asserts `elapsed < targets × perTarget`; verified it fails (1.09s vs 0.58s) with the ceiling disabled.

**Double `git merge-base` — all four agents converged.** One `CompareMetadataWithRemote` classifier now derives absent/aligned/ahead/behind/diverged/disconnected from a single merge-base; `IsMetadataDisconnected` is a wrapper and `MetadataDivergence` is gone. Doctor classifies once. The two verdicts can no longer disagree.

**Cache outlived its invocation.** `entire mcp` is a `for sc.Scan()` server on main's context, so my "cannot outlive the invocation" comment was false for a whole agent session — its `entire_status` tool would serve a stale remote list for hours. Added `WithFreshGitRemoteCache`, called per MCP request. Also corrected the claim that `applyMirrorRemotePlan` performs one mutation (it does two).

**Misattributed doc comment** — `checkDisconnectedMetadata`'s doc had ended up heading `reportMetadataDivergence`, leaving the repair function undocumented.

**Stale contract** — `CheckpointReadRemotes` still said "deliberately un-memoized" after I memoized underneath it; now states the split (git reads yes, settings and the captured-election file no) and why that's load-bearing for #1991.

perf(checkpoint): bound the read chain and stop re-electing per call

Fixes two costs this PR's read-candidate chain introduced, both measured
against origin/main with a PATH-shimmed git counting subprocesses.

Unbounded worst case. Per-candidate budgets replaced single shared ones —
a real fix, since one shared budget let a hung leader starve the legacy
origin tier — but nothing bounded the total, and these read paths have no
outer deadline: `entire resume` sets none and main() uses
context.WithCancel, not WithTimeout. fetchBlobsByHash lost the most: it
used to run inside one 2-minute budget that also covered its fallback
fetches, and per-target budgets left those fallbacks on the caller's
uncapped context, so a stalled hydration could spend per-target budgets
and then a fresh per-candidate metadata chain on top.

ReadChainBudget now wraps all three chains — checkpoint ref hydration, the
metadata branch chain, and blob hydration including its fallbacks — with
per-candidate budgets nested inside, so every candidate keeps its own
window while the total stays bounded.

Sized as an absolute 3 minutes rather than "n tiers x one full window".
The multiple is the trap: at 2 x ReadFetchTimeout with today's two tiers
the ceiling equals the loop's own worst case, so it cannot bind and buys
nothing, and blob hydration's fallbacks inherit an already-expired
context. An absolute ceiling binds for every chain of two or more
candidates, leaves a single-candidate chain untouched, and does not go
quietly wrong when a third tier appears. ReadChainLoopBudget holds back a
sixth of it so the fallbacks are funded rather than merely inside it, and
ReadFetchTimeout is exported so the cli-side paths stop carrying their own
2-minute literals that had to stay silently equal to it.

Election cost per command. The election re-runs on every call by design,
and each run shells out to git twice over .git/config: which remotes
exist, and does remote X exist. One command elects several times —
`entire checkpoint list` resolves the chain four times (disconnection
warning, branch listing, the git-refs store's remote discovery, imported
rewind points), spending 15 git subprocesses where main spent 9.

WithGitRemoteCache memoizes only those two .git/config reads, installed on
the root context in main(). The election result, settings, and the
captured-election file stay uncached, so a write followed by a re-resolve
still sees the new value — #1991's capture keeps working, which caching the
election result would have silently broken. Context-scoped and opt-in, so
an uninstrumented context behaves exactly as before and tests cannot leak
one temp repo's remote list into another.

Process scope is not invocation scope for every command: `entire mcp`
serves an agent session from one context, so it installs a fresh cache per
request via WithFreshGitRemoteCache rather than pinning one snapshot of
"which remotes exist" for hours. `entire repo mirror use` is the only
git-remote mutation in the CLI and invalidates after its writes.

WarnIfMetadataDisconnected now takes the caller's context instead of
building context.Background(): the detached context ignored both interrupt
cancellation and the cache, re-shelling out for answers the caller already
had.

Measured, `entire checkpoint list`: main 9 subprocesses, this PR before
these changes 15, after 9 — the regression is fully recovered (1 config
--get-regexp and 2 remote get-url, same as main).

Tests: the ceiling test stalls every target under a production-shaped
ratio (ceiling below targets x per-target, which is what makes it bind)
and asserts the call returns in ~ceiling — 0.58s with the ceiling, 1.09s
and failing without. Cache tests cover opt-in behavior, empty lists as
real answers, negative caching, invalidation, and an end-to-end guard that
a remote added mid-invocation is visible to a later election after
invalidation.

Stacked on #1951 — base retargets to `main` automatically when that merges.

## Problem

A force-fetched metadata branch can rewrite the local primary ref: `SafelyAdvanceLocalRef` replays local commits onto the fetched tip when the two sides diverged. No checkpoint is lost, but the ref moves and the replayed commits get new hashes — and nothing said so anywhere. The whole advance/replay chain (`SafelyAdvanceLocalRef`, `replayLocalRefFromBase`, `replayDisconnectedLocalRef`, `replayLocalCommits`, `setRefHash`) had **zero** logging calls, so an after-the-fact investigation had no trace to follow.

This came out of asking why the metadata fetch refspec is force (`+refs/heads/…`). The force itself is correct and load-bearing — v1 diverges by design (OPF rewrite, condensation, reconciliation), and without `+` a diverged tracking ref cannot be fetched at all, so divergence detection would never see the remote tip. The gap was that the *consequence* was invisible.

## Change

**The replay leaves a trace.** `replayLocalCommits` records ref, pre-rewrite local tip, target tip, replayed-commit count and a `diverged`/`disconnected` reason before rewriting. Logged in the function that performs the rewrite, not in its callers, so a future third caller cannot silently skip it. `Info`, not `Debug` — the default level has to carry it to be findable in `.entire/logs/`. Metadata only, per the logging privacy rule.

**`entire doctor` reports DIVERGED** with both tips instead of a bare `OK`:

```
Metadata branches: DIVERGED
  Local and remote entire/checkpoints/v1 have both advanced since they last agreed.
    local:  8415df1ee184
    remote: 7c46565c7e7c  (origin)
  No action needed: the next fetch from this remote replays your local
  checkpoints onto its tip. No checkpoints are lost, but the local ref moves
  and the replayed commits get new hashes.
```

Divergence is the one state whose resolution rewrites the local ref, and no existing check reported it — `IsMetadataDisconnected` covers only the no-merge-base case, and ahead/behind needs no comment. The message respects #1951's confinement rule: against the elected sync remote it self-heals, but a diverged legacy-tier ref never advances the local ref, so it says so instead of promising a fix that will not come.

**Both verdicts from one classifier.** `CompareMetadataWithRemote` derives absent / aligned / local-ahead / remote-ahead / diverged / disconnected from a single `git merge-base`, and `IsMetadataDisconnected` becomes a wrapper. Computing them separately meant `entire doctor` read four refs and spawned two `merge-base` subprocesses on the same hash pair to answer one question, from two bodies that could drift apart. Measured: 2 → 1.
